```{r} #| label: setup #| message: false #| warning: false #| include: false library(tidyverse) library(scales) library(knitr) library(kableExtra) # fonts ---- library(extrafont) library(sysfonts) source("_common.R") # use font showtext::showtext_auto() # set theme ggplot2::theme_set(fmggp2::theme_batman( base_size = 14)) ``` ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="simple"} ## Theme: `theme_batman()` Graphs in this chapter use `fmggp2::theme_batman()`, using its default `"movie"` palette from Batman (1989): a black background, a gold bat signal frame and title, a dark brown plot area, silver text, orange, gold, steel, rust, and pale gold marks, and a DIN Condensed title. ::: :::: {.callout-note collapse="false" icon=false}
```{r} #| label: full_code_display #| eval: true #| echo: false #| warning: false #| message: false #| out-height: '60%' #| out-width: '60%' #| fig-align: right library(ggplot2) library(dplyr) set.seed(1989) batman_box <- tibble( week = 1:26, week_of = as.Date("1989-06-23") + 7 * (week - 1), gross = round(55 * exp(-0.25 * (week - 1)) * exp(rnorm(26, mean = 0, sd = 0.12)), 2)) labs_line <- labs(title = "Batman", caption = "Simulated data", subtitle = "Weekly box office, summer and fall 1989", y = "Weekly gross ($ millions)", x = "Week of") ggp2_line <- ggplot(data = batman_box, mapping = aes(x = week_of, y = gross)) + geom_line(color = "#F9BB2C", linewidth = 1) ggp2_line + labs_line ``` ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #02577A;"} **Requirements:** ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"} **✅ a numeric (continuous) variable** ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"} **✅ a numeric (date) variable** ::: :::: ## Description Line graphs display changes of a numeric quantitative variable (on the `y` axis) over time (on the `x` axis). ## Set up ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **PACKAGES:** ::: Install packages. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ```{r} #| label: pkg_code_line_graph #| code-fold: show #| eval: false #| echo: true #| warning: false #| message: false #| results: hide library(ggplot2) library(dplyr) # for tibble() and data manipulation ``` ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **DATA:** ::: Tim Burton's *Batman* opened on June 23, 1989, and the bat signal was everywhere that summer (t-shirts, hats, cereal boxes, and a soundtrack by Prince). Like most blockbusters, it made the most money in its first week and a little less every week after that. We'll simulate 26 weeks of box office gross (in millions of dollars) that start at \$55 million and shrink by about the same percent each week. Each week also gets a random nudge from `rnorm()`, because no week's ticket sales land exactly on the trend. Setting the seed with `set.seed()` means you'll get the same 26 weeks every time you run the code below. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ```{r} #| label: data_line #| code-fold: show #| eval: true #| echo: true set.seed(1989) batman_box <- tibble( week = 1:26, week_of = as.Date("1989-06-23") + 7 * (week - 1), gross = round(55 * exp(-0.25 * (week - 1)) * exp(rnorm(26, mean = 0, sd = 0.12)), 2)) glimpse(batman_box) ``` ::: ## Distribution A line graph connects each value to the one that came before it, so it's built to show *change*. For the Batman data, the question is how fast the weekly gross falls. The answer isn't a fixed number of dollars per week; it's a fixed *share* of the previous week. Below we'll move from the box office numbers, to a picture, to the formula. ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **COUNT IT:** ::: Start with the first six weeks. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ```{r} #| label: count_values_line #| code-fold: show #| eval: true #| echo: true head(batman_box, 6) ``` ::: The drop from week one to week two is about \$`r round(batman_box$gross[1] - batman_box$gross[2], 1)` million, but the drop from week five to week six is only about \$`r round(batman_box$gross[5] - batman_box$gross[6], 1)` million. The dollar drops keep shrinking, so we'll divide each week by the week before it instead (`ratio`). ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ```{r} #| label: count_summary_line #| code-fold: show #| eval: true #| echo: true batman_ratios <- batman_box |> mutate(ratio = gross / lag(gross)) batman_ratios |> summarise(median_ratio = median(ratio, na.rm = TRUE), total_gross = sum(gross)) ``` ::: The median ratio is about `r round(median(batman_ratios$ratio, na.rm = TRUE), 2)`, which means a typical week keeps about `r round(100 * median(batman_ratios$ratio, na.rm = TRUE))`% of the previous week's gross. The 26 weeks add up to about \$`r round(sum(batman_box$gross))` million. ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **DRAW IT:** ::: On a regular `y` axis the line drops fast and then flattens out, which makes the late weeks hard to read. Below we draw the same line on a log scale with `scale_y_log10()`. On a log scale, equal *ratios* are equal distances, so a gross that keeps the same share every week becomes a straight line (the wiggles are the random nudges). ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ```{r} #| label: draw_line #| code-fold: show #| eval: true #| echo: true ggplot(data = batman_box, aes(x = week_of, y = gross)) + geom_line(color = "#F9BB2C", linewidth = 1) + geom_point(color = "#E96A23") + scale_y_log10() + labs(x = "Week of", y = "Weekly gross ($ millions, log scale)") ``` ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **NAME IT:** ::: The weekly gross follows [exponential decay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_decay) with a random multiplier for each week: $$ \text{gross}_w = 55 \, e^{-0.25 (w - 1)} \, \varepsilon_w, \quad \log(\varepsilon_w) \sim \text{Normal}(0, \; 0.12) $$ Each week keeps $e^{-0.25} \approx 0.78$ of the week before, which is why the median `ratio` landed near 0.78. Taking the log of both sides turns the formula into a straight line, $\log(\text{gross}_w) = \log(55) - 0.25(w - 1) + \log(\varepsilon_w)$, which is the line we saw on the log scale. The random part is a [normal distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_distribution) on the log scale (a [lognormal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Log-normal_distribution) multiplier), the same one we used for the Beanie Babies in @sec-violin-plots. Try changing `-0.25` to `-0.10` in the code above and the movie has much longer legs. ## Grammar ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **CODE:** ::: - Create labels with `labs()` - Initialize the graph with `ggplot()` and provide `data` - Map `week_of` to `x` and `gross` to `y` - Add `geom_line()` (with a gold `color` and a thicker `linewidth`, because the default black line disappears into the Gotham night) ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ```{r} #| label: code_graph_line #| code-fold: show #| eval: false #| echo: true #| warning: false #| message: false #| out-height: '100%' #| out-width: '100%' labs_line <- labs(title = "Batman", caption = "Simulated data", subtitle = "Weekly box office, summer and fall 1989", y = "Weekly gross ($ millions)", x = "Week of") ggp2_line <- ggplot(data = batman_box, mapping = aes(x = week_of, y = gross)) + geom_line(color = "#F9BB2C", linewidth = 1) ggp2_line + labs_line ``` ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **GRAPH:** ::: ```{r} #| label: create_graph_line #| eval: true #| echo: false #| warning: false #| message: false #| out-height: '100%' #| out-width: '100%' #| layout-nrow: 1 labs_line <- labs(title = "Batman", caption = "Simulated data", subtitle = "Weekly box office, summer and fall 1989", y = "Weekly gross ($ millions)", x = "Week of") ggp2_line <- ggplot(data = batman_box, mapping = aes(x = week_of, y = gross)) + geom_line(color = "#F9BB2C", linewidth = 1) ggp2_line + labs_line ```
